## Description

`ASRgwas` is a comprehensive R package designed to perform Genome-Wide Association
Studies (GWAS) using the modelling flexibility available in
[**ASReml-R**](https://vsni.co.uk/software/asreml-r). This library assists with
preparing and auditing phenotypic and genomic data; fitting GWAS models and
identifying significant markers; and evaluating and exploring output.

Main features:

- Data preparation and quality control via `pre.gwas()`.
- Dataset auditing and diagnostics via `audit.gwas()`.
- GWAS model fitting via `gwas.asreml()`, with support for Gaussian and binomial
  responses, population structure correction (**Q matrix**) and genomic
  relationship matrix (**K matrix**).
- Backward elimination for final marker selection via `select.marker()`.

Additional features (visualisation and exploration):

- Manhattan plots via `manhattan.plot()`.
- Quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots via `qq.plot()`.
- Phenotype-by-genotype plots for selected markers via `marker.plot()`.
- Genetic map visualisation via `map.plot()`.

## Installation

You can install `ASRgwas` from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

```{r installation, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_url("https://github.com/VSNinternational/asrgwas/releases/latest/download/ASRgwas_latest.tar.gz")
```

### Dependencies

`ASRgwas` depends on **R (>= 4.3.0)** and on the following packages:
`cli`, `data.table`, `ggplot2`, `ggrepel`, `Matrix`, `methods`, `stringr`,
`parallel`, `Rcpp`,
[`ASRgenomics`](https://github.com/VSNinternational/asrgenomics/releases/latest/download/ASRgenomics_latest.tar.gz) (>= 1.1.5), and
[`ASRtools`](https://github.com/VSNinternational/asrtools/releases/latest/download/ASRtools_latest.tar.gz).

> **Note on ASReml-R:** the core GWAS model fitting relies on
> [**asreml**](https://vsni.co.uk/software/asreml-r), a commercial package
> available from VSN International. A valid licence is required. Install it
> separately before using `gwas.asreml()`.

## Loading the package

Once installed, load the package as usual:

```{r load}
library(ASRgwas)
```

A quick check that the package is ready:

```{r check, eval = FALSE}
?ASRgwas
ls("package:ASRgwas")
```

## Overview

This tutorial organises the `ASRgwas` workflow into four steps:

1. **Prepare** — quality-control and match phenotypic and genomic datasets with `pre.gwas()`.
2. **Fit** — run the GWAS scan across all markers with `gwas.asreml()`.
3. **Select** — refine the set of significant markers via backward elimination with `select.marker()`.
4. **Explore** — visualise and interpret results with `manhattan.plot()`, `qq.plot()`, `marker.plot()`, and `map.plot()`.

### 1. Input data

`ASRgwas` works with three complementary objects.

The **phenotypic data frame** `pheno.data` must contain at least one column
identifying the individuals (genotypes) and one numeric column with the response
variable. Additional fixed effects, random effects, and covariates can be included
as extra columns.

The **genotype matrix** `geno.data` must be a numeric matrix with **individuals
on the rows** and **SNP markers on the columns**. Row names hold the individual
identifiers and column names hold the marker identifiers. Allele dosages are
encoded as **`0`**, **`1`**, and **`2`** (copies of the alternative allele),
with **`NA`** for missing calls.

The **genomic map** `map.data` is a `data.frame` with exactly three columns:
**`marker`** (matching the column names of `geno.data`), **`chrom`** (chromosome
identifier), and **`pos`** (physical or genetic position).

The package ships with three demonstration datasets from
[Nsibi *et al.* (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.120.401437) — an apricot
(*Prunus armeniaca*) F1 population of 155 genotypes and 60,991 SNPs — which can
be loaded as shown below and used as a template throughout this guide.

```{r datasets}
# Example datasets shipped with the package
data(pheno.apricot)  # phenotypic data frame (153 individuals, 9 traits)
data(geno.apricot)   # genotype matrix (155 individuals × 60,991 SNPs)
data(map.apricot)    # genomic map (60,991 markers)
```

### 2. Preparing data with `pre.gwas()`

`pre.gwas()` is the data preparation step. It checks, corrects, and matches the
phenotypic and genomic inputs and automatically generates the objects required by
`gwas.asreml()`: the genomic relationship matrix **K**, its inverse **Kinv**, and
the population structure matrix **Q** obtained via principal component analysis.

```{r pre-gwas-simple}
# Simple run with default QC filters.
gwas.data <- pre.gwas(
  pheno.data = pheno.apricot, indiv = "Ind", resp = "Sucrose",
  geno.data  = geno.apricot)
```

Additional quality-control filters and procedures can be passed directly via `...`.
Run `pre.gwas()` with no arguments to see the full list of available options
(forwarded from `ASRgenomics`):

```{r pre-gwas-args, eval = FALSE}
# List all accepted arguments.
pre.gwas()
```

A more complete call applying marker filtering, SNP pruning, and imputation:

```{r pre-gwas-full, eval = FALSE}
gwas.data <- pre.gwas(
  pheno.data = pheno.apricot, indiv = "Ind", resp = "Sucrose",
  geno.data  = geno.apricot, map.data = map.apricot,
  # QC options forwarded to ASRgenomics
  maf = 0.05, marker.callrate = 0.40,
  pruning.thr = 0.95, by.chrom = TRUE,
  impute = TRUE)
```

`pre.gwas()` returns a named list with (by default) all eight components:
`pheno.data`, `geno.data`, `K`, `Kinv`, `map.data`, `Q`, `plot.scree`, and
`eigenvalues`. Pass a character vector to the `return` argument to request only
a subset.

```{r pre-gwas-ls}
# Inspect returned objects
ls(gwas.data)
```

```{r pre-gwas-scree}
# Scree plot of principal components
gwas.data$plot.scree
```

```{r pre-gwas-eigen}
# Eigenvalues table
head(gwas.data$eigenvalues)
```

Alternatively, `audit.gwas()` can be used in place of `pre.gwas()` when the
user has already constructed the required objects externally and simply wants to
verify that all attributes and formats are suitable for `gwas.asreml()`:

```{r audit-gwas}
audit.gwas(
  pheno.data = gwas.data$pheno.data, indiv = "Ind", resp = "Sucrose",
  Kinv = gwas.data$Kinv, geno.data = gwas.data$geno.data,
  map.data = gwas.data$map.data, Q = gwas.data$Q)
```

### 3. Fitting GWAS models with `gwas.asreml()`

`gwas.asreml()` is the main function of `ASRgwas`. It extends ASReml-R to perform
a genome-wide scan by fitting, for each marker, a mixed model that can include
fixed effects, random effects, population structure (**Q**), and a genomic
relationship matrix (**K**).

#### 3.a. Base model (no marker scan)

It is good practice to first fit the base model — without any marker — to evaluate
the model structure and heritability before running the full scan.

```{r gwas-base, eval = has_asreml}
gwasA <- gwas.asreml(
  pheno.data = gwas.data$pheno.data,
  resp       = "Sucrose",
  gen        = "Ind",
  fixedf     = "Lots",
  residual   = "Lots",
  Kinv       = gwas.data$Kinv,
  Q          = gwas.data$Q,
  npc        = 3)
```

```{r gwas-base-call, eval = has_asreml}
# Inspect the model call
gwasA$call
```

```{r gwas-base-h2vc, eval = has_asreml}
# Heritability estimates (VC methods)
gwasA$heritability$h2.vc
```

```{r gwas-base-h2pev, eval = has_asreml}
# Heritability estimates (PEV methods)
gwasA$heritability$h2.pev
```

```{r gwas-base-aov, eval = has_asreml}
# ANOVA table
gwasA$aov
```

#### 3.b. Full GWAS scan

Once the base model is satisfactory, supply `geno.data` and `map.data` to trigger
the marker-by-marker scan. By default, `P3D = TRUE` is used ("Population
Parameters Previously Determined"), which fixes the variance components from the
base model and provides a considerable speed gain.

```{r gwas-full, eval = has_asreml}
gwasA <- gwas.asreml(
  pheno.data = gwas.data$pheno.data,
  resp       = "Sucrose",
  gen        = "Ind",
  fixedf     = "Lots",
  residual   = "Lots",
  Kinv       = gwas.data$Kinv,
  Q          = gwas.data$Q,
  npc        = 3,
  geno.data  = gwas.data$geno.data,
  map.data   = gwas.data$map.data,
  pvalue.thr = 0.0005,
  bonferroni = FALSE,
  workspace  = "2Gb")
```

```{r gwas-all, eval = has_asreml}
# Results for all tested markers
head(gwasA$gwas.all)
```

```{r gwas-sel, eval = has_asreml}
# Significant markers only
head(gwasA$gwas.sel)
```

`gwas.asreml()` returns a list of class `gwas.asreml` with six components:
`call`, `gwas.all`, `gwas.sel`, `mod`, `aov`, and `heritability`.
`gwas.all` contains one row per marker with columns `marker`, `chrom`, `pos`,
`maf`, `effect`, `z.ratio`, `p.value`, and `expl.var` (proportion of genetic
variance explained). `gwas.sel` is the subset of `gwas.all` with
`p.value < pvalue.thr` (after Bonferroni correction if `bonferroni = TRUE`).

### 4. Visualising results

#### Q-Q plot

`qq.plot()` generates a quantile-quantile plot of observed versus expected
*p*-values, which helps detect systematic inflation or deflation in the GWAS
statistics.

```{r qq-plot, eval = has_asreml}
qq.plot(gwas.table = gwasA$gwas.all)
```

#### Manhattan plot

`manhattan.plot()` displays the −log₁₀(*p*-value) for every marker across the
genome. Significant markers above the threshold are highlighted, and any candidate
regions can be annotated via `tag.table`.

```{r manhattan-plot, eval = has_asreml}
manhattan.plot(
  gwas.table = gwasA$gwas.all,
  pvalue.thr = 0.0005,
  padding    = 2e6)
```

When multiple GWAS analyses are stacked in a single `data.frame`, the
`gwas.index`, `facet.main`, and `facet.secondary` arguments control faceting
across panels.

#### Genetic map

`map.plot()` draws a karyotype-style view of the chromosomes with marker
positions. Selected markers can be highlighted via `tag.markers`.

```{r map-plot, eval = has_asreml}
map.plot(
  map.data    = gwas.data$map.data,
  tag.markers = gwasA$gwas.sel$marker)
```

#### Phenotype-by-genotype plots

`marker.plot()` generates boxplots or violin plots of the phenotypic response
stratified by genotypic dosage class (0 / 1 / 2) for a set of markers. These
plots help verify the biological plausibility of detected associations.

```{r marker-plot, eval = has_asreml}
# Subset genotype matrix to significant markers
sign.markers   <- gwasA$gwas.sel$marker
geno.data.sel  <- gwas.data$geno.data[, sign.markers, drop = FALSE]

marker.plot(
  pheno.data    = gwas.data$pheno.data,
  indiv         = "Ind",
  resp          = "Sucrose",
  geno.data.sel = geno.data.sel,
  type.plot     = "boxplot")
```

### 5. Selecting final markers with `select.marker()`

`select.marker()` refines the set of significant markers identified by
`gwas.asreml()` using backward elimination. Starting from a model that includes
all candidate markers as fixed covariates, it iteratively drops the marker with
the highest *p*-value until all remaining markers are below the chosen threshold.

```{r select-marker, eval = has_asreml}
set <- select.marker(
  gwas.object   = gwasA,
  geno.data.sel = geno.data.sel,
  ref.vc        = 1,
  pvalue.thr    = 0.1)
```

```{r select-call, eval = has_asreml}
# Final model call
set$call
```

```{r select-aov, eval = has_asreml}
# ANOVA table for the selected model
set$aov
```

```{r select-sel, eval = has_asreml}
# Final retained markers
set$gwas.sel
```

```{r select-var, eval = has_asreml}
# Proportion of genetic variance explained by the final set
set$expl.var
```

`select.marker()` returns a list with `call`, `gwas.sel`, `mod`, `aov`,
`expl.var`, and (when collinearity is an issue) `collinear.markers`.
